query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX (X = Si, Mn, or Al) high‐entropy alloys, achieving a homogeneous single‐phase solid solution enables controlled outward diffusion of the passivating element (Al or Si) leading to the rapid formation of a thin, coherent, and protective oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C, whereas multiphase microstructures, with their interphase boundaries, accelerate diffusive transport and promote the formation of thicker, porous oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CrFeCoNi alloy with a targeted substitution of X (where X is Si, Mn, or Al), processed to yield either a uniform single‐phase solid solution or a multiphase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Introduce the X element via alloying and tailor the processing route to control the microstructure (single‐phase versus multiphase), then expose the samples to temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere.
generation.conditions: High-temperature oxidation tests conducted above 900 °C (e.g., 900–1100 °C) under controlled oxygen-rich or corrosive environments (for example, atmospheres containing reactive species), over durations sufficient to develop measurable oxide scales (tens of hours).
generation.structural_mediator: The homogeneity of the microstructure governs the diffusion kinetics of the passivating elements; in a single‐phase alloy, reduced fast diffusion pathways (e.g., fewer grain boundaries) favor the formation of a uniform, adherent oxide layer, while multiphase structures with abundant phase boundaries enhance localized diffusion that leads to heterogeneous, stress‐prone scales.
generation.mechanism: In single‐phase alloys, the slower and uniform diffusion of Al or Si promotes the rapid formation of thermodynamically stable oxides (Al2O3 or SiO2, possibly mixed with Cr-oxides) that can remain adherent. In contrast, multiphase alloys provide preferential fast‐diffusion channels which lead to thicker, porous oxide scales with internal stresses that eventually crack or spall. Additionally, the intrinsic redox potentials of the X elements determine partner oxide phases with different stability, with Al and Si supporting protective scales and Mn favoring less protective, volatile oxides.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature oxidative or corrosive conditions, single-phase CrFeCoNiX alloys (particularly with X = Al or Si) will exhibit lower overall oxide growth rates, thinner and more coherent oxide scales, and reduced spallation compared to multiphase counterparts. In contrast, alloys with Mn as X are predicted to form less adherent and thicker, unstable oxide layers that crack under thermal stress.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNi alloy without the added X element or with nominal Mn content in a multiphase state, providing a reference for comparing oxide scale coherence, stability, and growth kinetics.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys operating in an environment above 900 °C under oxidizing or corrosive conditions; the results may vary with differences in processing methods, alloy design beyond the CrFeCoNiX system, or significant deviations in alloy composition.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds on evidence that Al substitution improves oxidation resistance via coherent Al-oxide scale formation (PMC9692591) and that microstructural refinement or single-phase conditions enhance diffusion-controlled protective scale formation (PMC9026100). Uncertainty remains in directly extrapolating these findings to CrFeCoNiX systems because exact diffusion coefficients, the interplay with other alloying elements, and scale stress dynamics may differ. The innovative element is extending the mechanistic role of microstructure from other HEA systems to the specific impact of X-element (Si, Mn, or Al) substitution in CrFeCoNi alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize equiatomic CrFeCoNiX (with X = Si, Mn, or Al) alloys processed to yield both single-phase and multiphase microstructures. Expose the specimens to high-temperature oxidation tests (900–1100 °C) in a controlled oxygen-rich or corrosive atmosphere for extended durations. Monitor oxide growth in situ using high-temperature XRD and ex situ through electron microscopy and oxidation weight gain measurements.
measurements: Mass gain and oxidation kinetics (via thermogravimetric analysis)
Oxide scale thickness and morphology (via SEM/EDS)
Phase identification and evolution (via in situ HT-XRD)
Adhesion and spallation resistance (via mechanical adhesion tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the single-phase alloys do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in oxide growth rate, enhanced scale coherence, and reduced spallation relative to the multiphase samples under the same conditions—or if the expected protective oxide compositions (e.g., Al2O3 or SiO2-based scales) are not observed for X = Al or Si—the hypothesis is falsified.

Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. Lu et al. reported the effect of Al content on the oxidation behavior of Y/Hf-doped AlxCoCrFeNi (x = 0.7, 1, 1.3) high-entropy alloys. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides.
